title: Parallel, intersecting, or skew?
intro: Two numbers settle every case: the cross product of the directions, and the shortest distance. Sort each pair.

cards.text: Two traces on the same PCB layer, both running along x at different y
Two aircraft holding the same heading at the same flight level, laterally offset
A pair whose common normal exists but whose computed distance is 0
Two conveyor paths crossing at the same height, meeting at the transfer point
One trace running along x on the top layer, another along y on the bottom layer
Two aircraft on crossing headings at different flight levels
A camera ray passing near a triangle's edge without touching it

debrief:
The aircraft appear three times, and that is the whole lesson. Same heading at the same level, laterally offset — **parallel**, constant separation, no conflict developing. Crossing headings at different levels — **skew**, and the only question that matters is the closest point of approach. If they were crossing at the *same* level they would **intersect**, which in air traffic is not a geometry result but an incident.

So the classification is not academic bookkeeping. It selects which computation is even meaningful: parallel lines need a different distance formula entirely, intersecting ones have a meeting point to solve for, and skew ones have a CPA and a time at which it occurs.

The PCB pair is the pleasing check. Top-layer x against bottom-layer y is skew, and the shortest distance between them comes out as exactly the dielectric thickness — 1.6 mm for standard FR4. When abstract geometry hands back a number you can measure with calipers, the method is working.
